title: A max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved to find the deepest point
summary: The assembler computes `max_stack` for a `Code` attribute: the deepest the operand stack gets, which for a straight-line sequence is the largest running sum of the instructions' stack effects. The loop compares the depth with the maximum after every instruction. A developer compares it only after an instruction that pushes more than it pops, since no other instruction can leave the stack deeper than it was. The property committed for the computation is the definition itself, `\max` over the prefix sums, written as nested JML quantifiers, under the assumption that the effects are those of JVM instructions. The prover checks the changed loop against it on every such sequence up to the bound; stated over every `int` effect instead, the same property refutes the change, on two effects whose sum wraps, which is the premise the developer's argument did not state.

change.description: Guard the comparison with the maximum by `delta[i] > 0`, so that the depth is compared only after an instruction with a positive stack effect; the comment says why that loses nothing. The tests for `max_stack` pass.

risk: The argument is short and the places where such arguments break are the ends, the zeros and the premises nobody wrote down: an empty sequence, a sequence that only pops, an instruction with effect 0, the maximum reached on the last instruction, and a depth that is an `int`. A `max_stack` one too small is rejected by the type checker at class load, on the first method that reaches the depth; a `max_stack` one too large is accepted and costs a slot. The tests cover an addition, a pair of longs, an empty method and a sequence whose deepest point is not its last.
explanation: The property committed for `of` is the definition of `max_stack` from JVMS §4.7.3 for a straight-line sequence, in JML: `result == (\max int k; 0 <= k && k <= delta.length; (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < k; delta[i]))`, the largest prefix sum, the empty prefix included so that a sequence that only pops has `max_stack` 0. The tool compiles the nested quantifiers to nested loops in the generated harness, one folding a maximum over the other's sums, and JBMC proves the changed loop against it on every sequence of up to eight effects in the range of JVM instructions, -255 to 2, which the property assumes: an invoke pops at most the 255 slots a descriptor may take, and nothing pushes more than two. That assumption was not in the first draft of the property, and without it the prover refuted the change in a second, on a sequence of two effects, shrunk from the seven the solver gave: two large negative numbers whose sum wraps below `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, so that the depth jumps to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` on a pop, which the original loop records and the changed loop, having seen a pop, does not. The developer's argument, that a pop cannot deepen the stack, is true of a stack and false of an `int`, and the proof found the premise. The assumption that makes it true is the one a JVM provides, it is on the page as part of the property, and the change is accepted under it because the specification holds of it, not because the old loop and the new one agree.
resolution: Merge, with the assumption. The definition stays as the property and the range of the effects as its premise; the next change to the loop, say one that tracks the depth in a `short`, is checked against both the same way.
notes: The array refutations of these Mica kernels are shrunk to a witness of one element.
`max_stack` is still the deepest point when the depth is checked only after a push: a safe change.
provenance: Constructed from the definition of max_stack in JVMS §4.7.3, applied to a straight-line sequence of stack effects.

references.title: JVMS §4.7.3, the Code attribute: max_stack is the maximum depth of the operand stack at any point during execution
